expansion:
A is correct: this is acute angle-closure glaucoma precipitated by systemic anticholinergic-induced mid-dilatation in a susceptible patient. The lecture identifies females and hyperopes as at risk, and lists “Use of systemic medications (anticholinergics)” among factors increasing risk through a mid-dilated pupil (L12, page 14). It describes the sequence from relative pupil block to iris bombe, narrowing of the anterior-chamber angle, impaired aqueous outflow, and a rapid severe rise in IOP—an “Ocular emergency” (L12, page 18). Her pain, coloured haloes, rapidly reduced vision, nausea and headache fit the listed symptoms, including “Nausea / Vomiting” (L12, page 19). The markedly raised IOP and mid-dilated fixed pupil likewise match the listed signs: “IOP → ++++ (stony hard)” and “Mid-dilated vertically oval non-reactive pupil” (L12, page 20).

B is wrong because optic neuritis is an optic-nerve disorder, not medication-triggered closure of the anterior-chamber angle with an abrupt IOP rise and a mid-dilated non-reactive pupil. The course associates acute optic neuritis with a central scotoma (L21, slide 4); the features in this vignette instead directly reproduce the acute-angle-closure clinical picture.

C is wrong because rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is caused by a retinal tear/break, whereas the course describes its typical symptoms as floaters, flashes, and a peripheral “curtain” or shadow (L20, slide 11). Those are not the acute painful, high-IOP, pharmacologically precipitated presentation here.

D is wrong because central retinal artery occlusion has retinal vascular signs—retinal whitening, a cherry-red macular spot, and marked APD—with VA < 6/60 (L19.2, page 26). It does not explain the narrow angles, anticholinergic trigger, mid-dilated fixed pupil, or markedly elevated IOP.
objective: Recognize that systemic anticholinergics can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma in a hyperopic patient with narrow angles.
